chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Abu Wallad, who said:
Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said: Verily God created a veil of darkness from what adjoins the east, and He appointed an angel over it.

So when the sun sets, that angel scoops a handful with his hand, then faces the west with it following the twilight and releases it little by little from his hands, and continues until he reaches the west at the disappearance of the twilight, whereupon he releases the darkness.
Then he returns to the east. When the dawn rises, he spreads his two wings and drives the darkness from the east to the west until the west is completed with it at the rising of the sun.

key_terms.الشَّفَق: Twilight/afterglow — the reddish glow after sunset whose disappearance marks the Maghrib prayer time
key_terms.الْفَجْر: Dawn — the break of dawn marking the time for Fajr prayer
key_terms.حِجَاب: Veil/curtain — a barrier of created darkness stored in the east
key_terms.مَلَك: Angel — a celestial being entrusted with managing the movement of darkness

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Sadiq say about the angel that manages darkness and the time for Maghrib prayer?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) describes the cosmological mechanism by which an appointed angel manages the transition from day to night and night to day. The hadith explains that darkness is a created veil stored in the east, which the angel releases gradually at sunset following the twilight, marking the time for Maghrib prayer when the twilight disappears. At dawn, the angel drives this darkness westward, completing the cycle at sunrise. This narration was understood by the original audience as both a theological description of divine order in creation and a practical guide establishing the prayer times of Maghrib and Fajr.
